edges.description: Kv1.4 encodes one component of the neuronal A-type potassium current, so loss of Kv1.4 function is expected to reduce that component. This has been shown for Kv1.4 knockout cortical neurons in mouse, not for the R89Q variant in human neurons.

KCNA4 transcript is present in the mouse lens, but how Kv1.4 loss leads to cataract is unknown. The authors speculate that loss of lens fibre and epithelial potassium conductance could disturb the lens microcirculation, and state that this has not been tested.

The authors propose that the striatal thinning reflects early neuronal death, by analogy with the greater ischaemic vulnerability of cultured striatal neurons from mice lacking Kv1.4 and Kv4.2. This link is a hypothesis; it has not been tested for KCNA4 deficiency.
Impaired cognition is present in all four patients, but how Kv1.4 loss of function causes it is not known.
ADHD is present in all four patients; no source proposes a specific mechanism, so the edge records only that the neuronal channel deficit is the presumed origin.
Dystonia, cogwheel rigidity and dystonic posturing are extrapyramidal signs and are attributed here to the striatal abnormality; neither report tests this link directly.

edges.limitations: Complete null allele, whereas the human R89Q allele reduces current only partly; mouse rather than human.

nodes.description: The homozygous missense variant NM_002233 c.266G>A p.(Arg89Gln) lies in a low-complexity segment of the Kv1.4 N-terminus, outside the inactivation, tetramerisation and pore domains. In Xenopus oocytes the mutant channel gave a smaller mean whole-cell current than wild type (14 versus 17 microamperes) while keeping rapid inactivation, which the authors interpret as a partial loss of function. Co-expression with wild type also lowered current, but the parents are unaffected heterozygotes.

nodes.description: Kv1.4 is a rapidly inactivating channel that contributes to the fast repolarising phase of neuronal action potentials and is present in striatal neurons, cortex, hippocampus and substantia nigra. Its expected cellular consequence is a smaller Kv1.4-encoded component of the A-type current; this has not been measured in patient-derived neurons.
